item.title: Automated TLS-Enabled Edge Server Configuration using MacBook and Docker Caddy
item.description:
To safely expose local devices externally in an on-premises or edge environment, establishing domain name resolution, router packet routing, and an automated TLS certificate renewal mechanism is essential. Conventional dynamic VirtualHost configurations or certbot-based cron management methods suffer from a rapid increase in configuration complexity as node count grows, posing a risk of service disruptions due to certificate renewal failures.

This article explains an end-to-end architecture that establishes automated HTTPS encrypted communication by deploying Docker and a Caddy reverse proxy on a MacBook host, integrated with public DNS (such as Gabia) and port forwarding.

Architecture Configuration and Traffic Flow

Requests to public domains are routed to the application layer inside the container in the following order:

[Client Browser]
 │
 ▼
[Public DNS Resolution] (Gabia A Record)
 │
 ▼
[Public WAN IP] (ISP Router / Gateway)
 │
 ▼
[Port Forwarding] (External 80/443 -> MacBook LAN IP)
 │
 ▼
[MacBook Host OS] (Home Server)
 │
 ▼
[Caddy Reverse Proxy Container] (Port 80 / 443 / 443 UDP)
 │
 ▼
[Application Container] (Bridge Network: custom-proxy)

1. Network Infrastructure and Port Forwarding

The MacBook within the local network is assigned a private IPv4 address via DHCP. To allow external traffic to reach the MacBook, port forwarding must be configured on the ISP router (gateway).

Checking Public WAN IP and Double NAT

Run the following command in the MacBook terminal to obtain the externally exposed public IPv4 address:

curl ifconfig.me

Log into the router management interface and verify that the displayed WAN IP address matches the output of curl ifconfig.me.

  • Double NAT Note: If the router’s WAN IP differs from the ifconfig.me result, a Double NAT topology exists where an upstream modem or router is present. In this scenario, external packets will not reach the MacBook unless port forwarding is also configured on the upstream gateway.

Router Port Forwarding Rules

Add the following forwarding rules in the router management interface:

  • HTTP: External Port 80 -> MacBook Private IP / Internal Port 80
  • HTTPS: External Port 443 -> MacBook Private IP / Internal Port 443

Necessity of Opening Port 80

Even if the application exclusively uses HTTPS (443), port 80 must remain open. Caddy automatically retrieves TLS certificates from Let’s Encrypt / ZeroSSL using the ACME (Automated Certificate Management Environment) protocol. This is required because the Certificate Authority accesses port 80 of the domain during the HTTP-01 challenge verification process.

2. DNS Record Configuration and Propagation Verification

Configure an A record pointing to the obtained public IPv4 address from the management console of your public DNS service (such as Gabia).

DNS Records to Configure

  • Host @ / Type A / Value [Public IPv4 Address]
  • Host www / Type A / Value [Public IPv4 Address]
  • Host * / Type A / Value [Public IPv4 Address] (Wildcard for subdomains)

Verification of DNS Propagation

Verify whether the configured records have propagated correctly using the dig utility:

# Query using the local default DNS
dig +short your-domain.com A

# Directly query Cloudflare's public DNS (1.1.1.1)
dig @1.1.1.1 your-domain.com A +short

If NXDOMAIN or SERVFAIL is returned, DNS record propagation is not complete. Wait until the response matches the router’s public IP address.

3. Reverse Proxy Configuration with Docker and Caddy

While Nginx requires combining certbot or external timers for TLS certificate acquisition and auto-renewal, Caddy handles certificate requests, verification, and automated renewal natively as a single unit.

Definition of `docker-compose.yml 

services:
 caddy:
 image: caddy:2
 container_name: caddy-server
 restart: unless-stopped
 ports:
 - "80:80"
 - "443:443"
 - "443:443/udp" # For HTTP/3 (QUIC) support
 volumes:
 - ./Caddyfile:/etc/caddy/Caddyfile:ro
 - ./data/caddy:/data
 - ./data/config:/config
 networks:
 - custom-proxy

networks:
 custom-proxy:
 external: true
 name: custom-proxy

Infrastructure Configuration Notes

  1. External Network (external: true): By manually pre-creating the custom-proxy network via CLI, backend containers spawned from other independent docker-compose.yml projects can also join the same proxy network.

    docker network create custom-proxy

  2. TLS Data Persistence (./data/caddy): Obtained certificates, private keys, and ACME account information are saved in the /data volume. Deleting this directory forces new certificate issuance upon every container restart, creating a risk of hitting Let’s Encrypt duplicate issuance Rate Limits and causing temporary service unavailability.

Caddyfile Creation and Routing Configuration

Create a test Caddyfile to verify proxy operations:

your-domain.com {
 respond "Home Server is running!" 200
}

Start the container:

docker-compose up -d

When forwarding to a backend application container in a production environment, configure the reverse_proxy directive as follows:

your-domain.com {
 reverse_proxy my-app:3000
}

With this setup, HTTP/HTTPS access to your-domain.com is automatically proxied to port 3000 of the my-app container on the internal Docker network custom-proxy.

Troubleshooting

1. Connection Failure due to Hairpin NAT (NAT Loopback)

Symptom: Access via the domain works normally from external networks (such as mobile cellular connections), but accessing https://your-domain.com from a device within the same LAN results in a timeout or connection error.

Cause: If a commercial router does not support Hairpin NAT (NAT Loopback), packets sent by clients inside the LAN to the router’s own public IP cannot be looped back and forwarded internally, causing the packets to be dropped.

Resolution and Countermeasures:

  • Always perform connection testing from an external network (mobile data communication or tethering).
  • For access within the LAN, bypass this issue by implementing a split-DNS configuration where a local DNS server (such as Pi-hole) or hosts file resolves the domain name directly to the MacBook’s private IP address.

2. System Operational Status and Verification Logs

The following are example output results for network socket status, Docker container status, DNS response, and HTTP response after system deployment:

$ docker ps --format "table {{.Names}}	{{.Status}}	{{.Ports}}"
NAMES STATUS PORTS
caddy-server Up 12 minutes 0.0.0.0:80->80/tcp, 0.0.0.0:443->443/tcp, 0.0.0.0:443->443/udp

$ ss -tulpn | grep -E ':(80|443)'
tcp LISTEN 0 4096 0.0.0.0:80 0.0.0.0:* users:(("docker-proxy",pid=14201,fd=4))
tcp LISTEN 0 4096 0.0.0.0:443 0.0.0.0:* users:(("docker-proxy",pid=14225,fd=4))
udp UNCONN 0 0 0.0.0.0:443 0.0.0.0:* users:(("docker-proxy",pid=14249,fd=4))

$ dig @1.1.1.1 your-domain.com A +short
203.0.113.42

$ curl -I https://your-domain.com
HTTP/2 200 
server: Caddy
content-type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
date: Thu, 05 Nov 2026 10:15:30 GMT

Key Takeaways

  • 💡 Necessity of Port 80 in ACME Verification: To achieve TLS automation, port forwarding for port 80 (used for the HTTP-01 challenge) is essential alongside port 443 for HTTPS communication.
  • ⚠️ Retention of Data Volumes: To avoid Let’s Encrypt rate limits, persistence of Caddy’s /data directory is critically important.
  • 🛠️ Network Isolation Design: Utilizing Docker external networks (external: true) enables secure and flexible communication between Caddy and multiple independent service containers.

item.title: Security Hardening and Network Infrastructure Implementation Essentials in Linux System Administration
item.description:
Security Hardening and Network Availability Optimization in Linux System Administration

In Linux system operation and management, security hardening and ensuring network availability are top priorities for infrastructure engineers. From strengthening authentication mechanisms to network layer redundancy and permission management in task automation, the practical technical specifications are organized below.

1. Advancing SSH Authentication Mechanisms: Implementation of Key-Based Authentication

Traditional password authentication is vulnerable to brute-force attacks and credential leaks. In contrast, key-based authentication using asymmetric encryption establishes an authentication model based on possession rather than knowledge, providing a high level of security.

1.1 Key Pair Structure and Authentication Workflow

The private key generated on the client side must be stored securely, and only the public key is registered in the server’s ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. The authentication process is executed via a challenge/response method involving connection requests, authentication challenges, digital signature creation using the private key, and signature verification with the registered public key.

1.2 Implementation Command Examples

In Linux environments, ssh-keygen is used to generate key pairs, which are then deployed under appropriate permission settings.

ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096
ssh-copy-id user@remote_host

2. Server Security Hardening and Auditing

Password complexity and the selection of hashing algorithms are the foundation of system defense. Current standard specifications recommend hashing using SHA-512 ($6$). These settings are controlled through /etc/login.defs or PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules) modules.

As part of security auditing by administrators, detecting weak passwords using tools like John the Ripper and static analysis of suspicious files using VirusTotal are effective. As an operational precaution, anti-phishing measures, such as verifying links hidden by URL shortening services like TinyURL, are also essential.

3. Communication Tunneling via SSH Port Forwarding

SSH tunneling is a technique for building another logical communication channel within an encrypted SSH session. This ensures a secure access path to ports restricted by firewalls.

3.1 Local Port Forwarding Implementation

This configuration forwards a specific port on the client side to a target host via a remote server.

ssh -L 8080:target_host:80 user@remote_host

4. Network Infrastructure Redundancy and Optimization

4.1 IP Aliasing (IP Binding)

Assigning multiple IP addresses to a single physical NIC enables virtual hosting and other functions. In environments like CentOS, temporary assignment is possible using specific interface configuration commands.

ifconfig eth0:0 192.168.1.100 netmask 255.255.255.0 up

4.2 Network Bonding (Channel Bonding)

Multiple physical NICs are integrated into a single logical interface to ensure bandwidth expansion and fault tolerance. The main modes are as follows:

  • Mode 0 (balance-rr): Load balancing via round-robin.
  • Mode 1 (active-backup): Only one NIC is active, with automatic failover to the standby system upon failure.
  • Mode 4 (802.3ad LACP): Link aggregation in coordination with a switch.

5. Granular Permission Management via FACL (File Access Control Lists)

For complex permission requirements that the standard owner/group/others model cannot handle, FACL is used to grant individual permissions to specific users or groups.

setfacl -m u:username:rwx /path/to/file
getfacl /path/to/file

6. Task Automation and Access Control: Cron and At

Cron is used for periodic backups and log rotations, while at is used for one-time executions. Execution permissions for these must be strictly managed via /etc/cron.allow and /etc/cron.deny.

6.1 Cron Configuration Specifications

The following configuration describes settings for automatically executing jobs based on a specific schedule.

# Execute backup script every day at 3:00 AM
00 03 * * * /usr/local/bin/backup.sh

7. Log Management and System Observability

Log data accumulated under /var/log/ is a lifeline for fault diagnosis. To prevent disk space exhaustion, proper generation management and compression using logrotate are essential. Additionally, real-time system monitoring using the watch command and measuring process execution time with the time command provide fundamental data for performance tuning.

Conclusion

The core of Linux system administration lies in the thorough application of the Principle of Least Privilege through SSH key authentication and FACL, combined with achieving both network flexibility and robustness through bonding and tunneling. By appropriately combining these technical elements, a secure and highly available infrastructure foundation can be realized.
